item.title: Compromised TLS Certificates
item.description: <p>The Indian CA eMudhra Limited has eight TLS certificates with <a href="https://arstechnica.com/security/2026/10/the-internet-goes-on-high-alert-after-discovery-of-8-compromised-tls-certs/">laughably weak private keys</a>:</p> <blockquote><p>The compromised eMudhra keys were defective at a level that’s challenging the imagination of many of the engineers studying the incident. A normal size for a NIST P-384 elliptic curve cryptography private key contains roughly 384 bits of entropy, a size allowing almost 2<sup>384</sup>, or a number with 116 digits, different possibilities. The private key sizes of the compromised keys ranged from 3 to 8 bits. Astonishingly, the private keys were 4, 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230, 237...</p></blockquote>
item.dc:creator: Bruce Schneier

item.title: Critical Flaw in Python’s Popular Pillow Image Library Allows Code Execution via a Crafted Image
item.description:
Pillow, the most widely used image library for Python, can be made to run operating system commands on a server by specifying the name of a file it is told to open.
The flaw,&nbsp;CVE-2026-112900, is in the way Pillow handles EPS images, which it opens by passing the file's name to Ghostscript, a separate program it runs to turn the image into pixels, without checking the name first.
